title: Karenni Resistance Group Pledges Non-Interference in Business, Governance
body:
The Karenni Nationalities Defence Force (KNDF), a major anti-junta resistance group in eastern Myanmar, will refrain from engaging in civilian administration or commercial enterprises, chairman Khun Bedu announced during the group’s inaugural conference.
Speaking to delegates at the conference held Aug. 28–29, Khun Bedu emphasized that building a strong organizational structure is essential to maintaining a disciplined military force focused solely on protecting civilians.
“I believe the most basic foundation for keeping the force strong and sustainable, while staying out of civilian administration and business, is to have a proper organizational structure,” Khun Bedu said. He added that the group remains committed to guiding its members toward a federal democracy grounded in equality and freedom from military dictatorship.
A primary strategic objective reaffirmed at the conference is unifying all armed factions operating in Karenni (Kayah) State into a single, professional state army.
“Our KNDF Central Committee has decided to keep working toward establishing a state army,” Khun Bedu noted. “This can only happen if we can work together with the political forces in the state and build trust with one another... That trust will become a strong driving force for establishing a state army.”
The two-day conference brought together 105 delegates—including Central Committee members, regional commanders, department heads, and battalion commanders- comprising 91 men and 14 women.
Participants reviewed the group’s military and political activities while adopting future roadmaps for organizational development and alliance-building within Myanmar’s broader resistance movement.

title: 16-Year-Old Sentenced to 10 Years for Child Rape and Murder in Western Myanmar
body:
A court in western Myanmar’s Rakhine State has sentenced a 16-year-old boy to 10 years in prison for the rape and murder of a toddler, sparking outrage from the victim’s family after authorities released his mother, who was accused of acting as an accomplice.
The Maungdaw District Court handed down the verdict on Sept. 4 under juvenile justice laws, which cap maximum penalties for underage offenders.
The teenager, identified as Maung Pauk Sa Chay, was convicted of sexually assaulting and killing his 2-year-old neighbor in Aung Thukha Village on March 16.
Following the attack, the suspect’s mother allegedly assisted in hiding the victim’s body in a sack.
The local Department of Law Enforcement and Public Security (DLEPS) initially detained both.
However, officials released the mother one month later, citing a lack of evidence.
The decision to release the mother and the short sentence handed to the youth drew sharp criticism from the victim's family, who announced plans to appeal to higher judicial authorities.
“The primary perpetrator who brutally killed a child was given only 10 years, while the court released his mother,” a male relative of the victim said. “This case lacks justice completely. We lost our daughter and failed to obtain true justice.”
While the family originally pressed charges for rape, robbery, murder, and concealment of a corpse, prosecutors proceeded only on murder and rape counts.
The trial featured testimony from 13 prosecution witnesses and four defense witnesses.
The sentencing highlights mounting concerns over judicial consistency in Rakhine State, where at least 13 cases of sexual violence against children have been recorded in 2026.
In a separate case in July, the Sittwe District Court sentenced a man to death for the rape and murder of a young woman in Ponnagyun Township, while handing 20-year prison terms to two co-conspirators.Photo: Illustration

title: Mon Resistance Group Launches Drug Crackdown in Southern Myanmar
body:
An anti-junta Mon ethnic resistance group has detained 42 people in a sweeping crackdown on drug trafficking aimed at curbing rampant substance abuse among local youth in southern Myanmar, officials and residents said Tuesday.
The New Mon State Party Anti-Dictatorship (NMSP-AD) launched the operations across its administrative areas, targeting major distributors and traffickers of illicit narcotics, including kratom leaves.
“The drug problem cannot simply be left as it is,” said Nai Thu Ya Htay, head of the NMSP-AD’s Northern Regional Command. “We consider it a major threat to our people, and we will continue arresting drug traffickers until they are no longer operating.” He added that traffickers will be prosecuted under regional laws, while drug users will receive education and rehabilitation support.
In recent weeks, NMSP-AD forces arrested three suspects—two men and one woman—in Htonman village and another woman in Kawtpihtaw village, both located in Mudon Township.
Residents expressed strong support for the crackdown, describing how illicit drugs have been sold openly to underage students near schools.
“The sellers don’t care whether the buyers are children or adults,” a Mudon resident said. “Children buy drugs before going to school and after school. That’s how bad things have become.”
Resistance officials accused Myanmar’s ruling military junta of deliberately allowing drug trafficking and gambling operations to flourish since the 2021 coup, alleging that regime forces collect taxes from dealers to weaken youth civic engagement and leadership in ethnic areas.

title: Fuel Prices Soar Near 4,000 Kyats per Liter in Myanmar’s Capital as Junta Mandates Import Cuts
body:
Fuel prices in Myanmar continue to surge, with official retail rates for standard gasoline approaching 4,000 kyats ($1.27) per liter in the military-controlled capital of Naypyitaw—and informal roadside prices jumping nearly double that amount as junta-mandated import restrictions take effect.
According to official reference prices published Sept. 13 by the junta’s Petroleum Product Regulatory Department (PPRD), 92 Octane reached 3,930 kyats per liter in Naypyitaw, while 95 Octane hit 4,055 kyats. Regular diesel rose to 4,255 kyats ($1.37) and premium diesel reached 5,155 kyats ($1.66).
The latest increases reflect a sharp rise since late August, with 92 Octane climbing more than 240 kyats per liter in just over two weeks. Similar spikes have hit major economic hubs, including Yangon and Mandalay.
On the black market, roadside vendors in Naypyitaw are selling one-liter bottles for as much as 7,000 kyats ($2.26).
The price hikes are straining daily operations and public services nationwide.
A non-CDM civil servant in the Bago Region said office generator fuel costs jumped from 500,000 kyats to 700,000 kyats ($226) during rolling power outages, forcing staff to slash field travel and rely on local villagers for transportation.
Myanmar is heavily reliant on foreign energy, importing roughly 95% of its fuel supply, according to a report by the Institute for Strategy and Policy (ISP Myanmar).
Despite chronic foreign currency shortages and frequent fuel panics since the 2021 coup, junta chief Min Aung Hlaing ordered a 30% reduction in foreign fuel imports beginning this month, claiming domestic refineries will offset the shortfall.

title: Junta Drone and Artillery Strike Kills Civilian in Eastern Myanmar
body:
A 40-year-old man was killed on Monday when Myanmar military forces targeted a village in Nanmehkhon Township—located along the border of Shan and Karenni (Kayah) states—with suicide drones and heavy artillery, according to residents.
The attack occurred around 3:30 p.m. on Sept. 14 near a village fuel station. Junta forces deployed two suicide drones and fired a heavy artillery shell without prior aerial reconnaissance, witnesses said.
The victim sustained fatal injuries to his head and arm.
The strike comes amid heightened safety warnings along the Shan-Karenni border.
The Mobye People’s Defense Force (PDF) recently urged civilians to avoid traveling on roads connecting western Mobye and Nanmehkhon due to frequent, heavy clashes between resistance forces and regime troops in the area.
Military aerial and drone bombardments have escalated sharply across Karenni State this month.
At least 10 civilians, including young children, have been killed by junta airstrikes in September across Nanmehkhon, Hpasaung, and Shadaw townships.

title: Myanmar Junta Airstrikes Destroy Thousands of Homes in Kachin’s Shwegu Township
body:
Thousands of homes across 18 villages in Kachin State’s Shwegu Township have been destroyed by Myanmar military airstrikes over the past six weeks, according to the local resistance-led Shwegu Township People’s Administration.
Regime forces initially launched ground offensives in June to retake territory controlled by the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and allied resistance forces. However, a counteroffensive by the KIA-led coalition forced junta troops to retreat to downtown Shwegu in July, where they remain stationed.
Following the retreat, the military unleashed daily bombardments across the township from August through September 10.
“Fighter jets have been dropping bombs two to three times a day,” an official from the Shwegu Township People’s Administration said. “Villages along both banks of the Ayeyarwady River and surrounding the town have been hit. In places like Lanku andMyaingthar, almost every house has been destroyed.”
Local sources report that Lanku, Myaingthar, Pantin, Zinbon, Weama, and Nanpaung have suffered near-total destruction. Other affected villages—including Thinbawinn, Moesit, Yaele, Bokone, Paukkone, Kyauktalone, Kyuntaw,Tawlang, Ngarbatgyi, Ngarbatwa, Kyaukkyi, and Shwegulay—have lost roughly half of their housing stock.
In addition to residential homes, airstrikes targeted civilian infrastructure unrelated to active combat, destroying schools, monasteries, and livestock.
The intensified air campaign follows failed regime efforts to resupply troops via the Ayeyarwady River. In late August, a 15-vessel junta flotilla attempting to transport reinforcements and supplies between Shwegu and Bhamo suffered heavy losses in riverine ambushes by KIA forces.
Several vessels were destroyed, and over 100 junta personnel were captured as prisoners of war.
The military currently controls only downtown Shwegu and its immediate surroundings, while resistance forces maintain control over most rural areas of the township. Shwegu previously suffered widespread damage in 2022 and 2023, when junta troops burned down nearly 30 villages during ground operations.

title: Junta Offer for Peace Talks Unlikely to Lead to Negotiations Soon, Kachin Analysts Say
body:
Recent reports indicating that the Myanmar military junta’s peace negotiation body, the National Solidarity and Peacemaking Negotiation Committee (NSPNC), has offered to hold talks with the Kachin Independence Organization (KIO) are unlikely to yield actual negotiations anytime soon, according to Kachin political analysts.
The reported offer comes as junta forces suffer major setbacks on the battlefield, including heavy damage to military flotillas entering Kachin State from central Myanmar.
Analysts suggest the junta’s overture stems from strategic desperation rather than a genuine desire for peace. Facing severe territorial losses across the country—most notably in Rakhine State, where combat against the Arakan Army (AA) has expanded into urban areas—the military regime may be attempting to secure a localized ceasefire in Kachin State to free up its resources.
"I think the junta is making this move because of its military setbacks," a Kachin political analyst told KNG. "While struggling with losses against the Arakan Army, it may be trying to negotiate a temporary halt to the fighting in Kachin State. If talks were to happen, the junta would likely have to make concessions and compromise."
However, analysts emphasize that formal dialogue remains improbable. Beyond the ongoing active combat, the KIO leadership has repeatedly reaffirmed its commitment to working alongside allied resistance forces to permanently dismantle the military dictatorship.
"The KIO chairperson has consistently emphasized the goal of uprooting the military dictatorship in public addresses," the analyst added. "It will be very difficult for the junta to negotiate with the KIO under these circumstances."
The report of the peace offer coincides with escalating combat in Kachin State's Shwegu Township. Resistance forces led by the Kachin Independence Army (KIA), the KIO's armed wing, have been mounting a sustained campaign to capture Bhamo, the state's second-largest city.
In response, the junta dispatched two reinforcement flotillas from Mandalay along the Ayeyarwady River in late August to break the siege. However, the operations have faced intense resistance:
First Flotilla: A 15-vessel convoy was ambushed near Hsinhkan Village between Shwegu and Bhamo. Resistance forces destroyed at least seven vessels and captured more than 150 junta prisoners of war (POWs).
Second Flotilla: On September 9, resistance forces destroyed three out of four advance vessels near Katha and Shwegu. Heavy riverine clashes remain ongoing.
"It will be difficult to start dialogue while fierce fighting is underway and the junta continues its offensive maneuvers," another political analyst noted. "Under these conditions, it is implausible for the KIO to travel to the capital, Naypyidaw, for negotiations."
The NSPNC reportedly extended a formal invitation dated September 4 for the KIO to send a delegation to Naypyidaw. However, Col. Naw Bu, spokesperson for the KIO/KIA, stated he was unaware of any such outreach. "I haven’t heard anything about that report, received no instructions, and have no comment," he said.
The KIO previously participated in the 2015 peace process but declined to sign the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) after the military excluded key members of the Northern Alliance of ethnic armed groups.
Following the February 2021 military coup, the KIO declared it would only participate in talks that inclusively feature the civilian-led National Unity Government (NUG) and all allied revolutionary bodies. Reaffirming this stance during the 65th Kachin Revolution Day in February 2026, KIO Vice Chairman-1 Lt. Gen. Sumlut Gun Maw questioned whether the junta was truly prepared to engage in talks that include the NUG.

title: Arakan Army Repels Junta Advances as Clashes Intensify Near Strategic Myanmar Port
body:
Heavy clashes continue across Kyaukphyu Township in western Myanmar’s Rakhine State as the Arakan Army (AA) repelled renewed military junta advances, seizing weapons, ammunition, and enemy casualties during recent engagements, according to military sources.
Intense fighting erupted on Sept. 9 and 10 when AA forces intercepted a junta column advancing from Awa Taung Village near the strategic Taung Maw Oo naval station.
Facing significant casualties, regime forces deployed airstrikes and naval artillery cover while AA troops captured military equipment, weapons, and several bodies left behind by junta soldiers.
Frequent skirmishes have continued around the naval base and surrounding villages, including Kyaungkho, Chaungphyar, and Minpyin.
“Junta warships are firing continuously as the regime desperately pushes ground offensives,” a local source said.
An earlier junta advance on Sept. 4 toward AA-controlled Sanae Town was also repelled, forcing regime troops to retreat after heavy losses.
Military defectors and analysts note that the regime is exploiting the AA’s restraint around Kyaukphyu—home to major Chinese deep-sea port and pipeline investments—to launch aggressive attacks.
“The only remaining ground footholds for the military regime in Arakan State are Sittwe and Kyaukphyu,” said Captain Zin Yaw, a military defector. “To leverage these strategic positions for future military or political gains, the regime will likely execute its most violent offensives here.”
Despite persistent junta probes supported by naval and air assets since mid-2025, the Arakan Army has maintained a defensive posture around Kyaukphyu to avoid escalating conflict near key infrastructure, while repeatedly repelling regime advances.
The ongoing violence has taken a severe toll on civilians. Indiscriminate aerial, drone, and naval bombardment has forced residents from numerous villages—including Zinchaung, Kyaukphyauk, Wamyaung, Ngaoak, and Kyaukkalay—to flee their homes repeatedly.
Since fighting first broke out in Kyaukphyu on Feb. 20, 2024, more than 60,000 internally displaced persons (IDPs) have been left in urgent need of humanitarian relief and basic supplies.

title: Ethnic Armed Groups in Myanmar Reject Junta Peace Overtures, Vow Coalition Unity
body:
Major ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) belonging to a key resistance coalition have rejected peace talk approaches from Myanmar's military junta, insisting on all-inclusive negotiations and adhering to their shared federal democratic framework.
The Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF)—formed on March 30 by the shadow National Unity Government (NUG), parliamentary body CRPH, and four major ethnic armies—reiterated its refusal to engage in separate, bilateral talks aimed at dividing the resistance movement.
Two central Myanmar resistance groups from Sagaing and Mandalay regions have also joined the coalition.
The junta recently attempted to approach the Chin National Front (CNF) through third-party intermediaries, sending representatives as far as Aizawl, India. However, the offer was rejected.
“The peace offers from coup leader Min Aung Hlaing are not genuine,” said Dr. Sui Khar, foreign minister of the Chinland Council government, during an Aug. 28 press briefing. “If he truly wants peace, he needs to offer inclusive talks involving all stakeholders. The junta’s approach of negotiating only with individual ethnic groups must not happen. That’s why we stand firmly by the principles of the SCEF.”
Meanwhile, the Kachin Independence Organization (KIO) addressed reports that the junta had invited it to peace talks on Sept. 4.
“We haven’t received any official information about this,” said Col. Naw Bu, spokesperson for the KIO and its armed wing, the Kachin Independence Army (KIA).
Col. Naw Bu previously emphasized that the KIO will not accept separate talks designed to sow division among anti-junta forces. But he said it remains open to comprehensive dialogue with all political stakeholders.
Other alliance members, including the Karenni National Progressive Party (KNPP) and the Karen National Union (KNU), have similarly rejected the junta's approach.
The KNPP stated it would refuse any talks predicated on the military-drafted 2008 Constitution or the 2015 Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA), both of which preserve the military's political dominance.
The NUG, CRPH, KIO, KNU, CNF, and KNPP established the SCEF to provide political and military leadership for the resistance movement.
The coalition's six core objectives include ending military rule, permanently removing the armed forces from politics, establishing civilian command over the military, completely abolishing the 2008 Constitution, drafting a new federal democratic charter, and pursuing transitional justice.

title: Five Years Post-Coup, Myanmar Sees No Progress Under Min Aung Hlaing, Analysts Say
body:
Five years after the February 2021 military coup, Myanmar continues to experience severe deterioration across its political, economic, healthcare, and education sectors, with little prospect of recovery under junta leader Min Aung Hlaing, political analysts and local figures say.
Despite recent efforts by Min Aung Hlaing to invite foreign investment through visits to China, Russia, and India after assuming the presidency following a controversial election, regional politicians say the country remains mired in conflict, inflation, and diplomatic isolation.
Foreign investment is unlikely to return anytime soon, a Mon politician told IMNA, contrasting current economic stagnation with the reform era under former President Thein Sein (2011–2016).
“I don’t see any prospect for economic growth,” the politician said. “During the Thein Sein era, there were discussions with ethnic armed organizations, state-level agreements, and eventually the Nationwide Ceasefire Agreement (NCA). I don’t see this administration making any comparable progress.”
A Kachin politician similarly criticized the regime for a complete lack of policy transparency, soaring commodity prices, and severe import-export disruptions.
“We see him traveling internationally, but domestically, there are no concrete peace efforts,” the Kachin figure said. “Under the current circumstances, prices are rising, and trade is struggling. We have not seen any open or transparent governance.”
Empirical data reflects this economic collapse. According to the independent think tank ISP-Myanmar, foreign direct investment (FDI) into Myanmar totaled more than $28.7 billion between 2016 and 2020.
In contrast, total FDI between 2021 and 2025 dropped to just $7.4 billion—meaning the entire five-year post-coup total was less than what Myanmar attracted in 2016 alone.
Foreign investors continue to avoid the country due to ongoing armed conflict, a breakdown in the rule of law, chronic power outages, hyperinflation, and volatile policies.
Meanwhile, military authorities and various armed groups are increasingly competing for control over critical border trade routes.
Another Myanmar political observer warned that relying on authoritarian allies will not resolve the nation's compounding crises, citing widespread corruption at all levels of government.
“There is no reason for things to get better,” the observer noted. “The present is grim, and the future looks worse. Aligning with China and Russia won't rescue us—they act strictly in their own interests.”

title: Over 150 Junta Troops Killed in Strategic Karen State Town, KNU Says
body:
More than 150 Myanmar military junta troops, including two officers, have been killed in Hpapun Township, eastern Myanmar’s Karen State, over the past three and a half months, according to the Karen National Union (KNU).
Under the KNU’s administrative structure, Hpapun falls within Mutraw District, the primary operational area of its armed wing, the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) Brigade 5.
Since early May, junta forces have launched offensives along the Hpapun-Kamarmaung Road, deploying heavy reinforcements to secure a strategic hilltop base and retake Hpapun Town, which regime forces lost control of earlier this year.
However, ambushes and coordinated attacks by the KNLA and allied resistance forces left 152 junta soldiers dead and roughly 200 others wounded, including deputy battalion commanders, Brigade 5 reported. An additional 36 regime soldiers deserted their units during the fighting.
“Over the past few months, the enemy has tried to break through, but they have suffered heavy losses,” said Padoh Saw Htoo Robin, spokesperson for Brigade 5. “We are releasing this information so the public knows the facts.”
In response to the military setbacks, junta forces escalated airstrikes and artillery bombardment against civilian areas along the Hpapun-Kamarmaung Road, setting several villages on fire.
The indiscriminate attacks killed four civilians, injured 22 others, and damaged 275 homes, 18 schools, and five religious buildings, according to the Mutraw District administration. Nearly 36,000 residents from 27 villages have been displaced by the ongoing conflict.
Meanwhile, pro-junta social media channels have mounted an aggressive disinformation campaign, claiming heavy resistance casualties while concealing the regime's own operational losses in the region.

title: Over 5,000 Displaced Civilians Face Urgent Food Shortage in Western Myanmar
body:
More than 5,000 civilians displaced by war in Kyaukphyu Township, western Myanmar’s Rakhine State, are in critical need of emergency food supplies as intense fighting continues between the Arakan Army (AA) and military junta forces.
The escalating violence has forced thousands of rural residents from their homes in recent weeks.
On Sept. 11, the Kyaukphyu-based Zin Chaung Youth Philanthropic Association reported that 5,100 displaced individuals urgently require food aid.
According to the organization, providing a basic monthly ration—calculated at two condensed-milk cans of rice per person daily, or two baskets per month—requires 10,200 baskets of rice monthly. At current market prices of 16,000 kyats per basket, the total monthly cost is estimated at 163.2 million kyats (around $43,000).
Residents expressed deep concern over the looming threat of starvation.
“We Arakanese people hold a deep sense of dignity and find it difficult to ask for donations,” Ko Khin Kyaw Nyunt, a resident, told Narinjara. “However, in times of such extreme hardship, we must set aside our pride to save lives. I earnestly appeal to international philanthropic organizations to help the thousands displaced in Kyaukphyu.”
The aid group emphasized that the crisis extends far beyond this immediate group. Emergency food is urgently needed for roughly 30,000 displaced people scattered across eight camps in Kyaukphyu Township, plus tens of thousands who fled to neighboring Ramree Township.
Across both townships, the total number of displaced people facing severe food insecurity now exceeds 50,000.
A local relief organization confirmed to Narinjara that it is currently coordinating logistics to deliver emergency food supplies to the most vulnerable 5,100 individuals.

title: Paddy Prices Surge in Myanmar’s Mon State Ahead of Monsoon Harvest
body:
Paddy prices across all varieties have surged in Mon State ahead of the upcoming monsoon harvest, driven by shrinking market stocks, high demand, and widespread flood damage, local farmers said.
Prices for unhusked rice (paddy) now range from 4 million to 5 million kyats per 100 baskets (roughly 2.1 metric tons), depending on the variety.
A farmer from Paung Township told the Independent Mon News Agency (IMNA) that local stocks are nearly exhausted as growers were forced to sell early to raise working capital for planting.
“Prices jumped by more than 500,000 kyats in just one week, but there is hardly any paddy left to sell,” the farmer said. “When we needed cash for farming, we started selling at around 3.5 million kyats. By the time it hit 4 million, most farmers had already sold off their stock.”
Prices vary across districts, however, and some farmers are holding onto their remaining yield in anticipation of further price hikes.
“In our village, no one has sold their stored paddy yet,” said a farmer from Kyaikmaraw Township. “We plan to sell before the new monsoon crop arrives. If prices rise above current levels, we’ll sell, but for now, we’re holding out.”
Soaring input costs—particularly for fuel and fertilizer—have sharply reduced the acreage planted for this year’s monsoon crop. Farmers say sustained high prices are essential if farming is to remain financially viable next season.
“Everything, including land preparation, has become far more expensive,” explained a farmer from Mudon Township. “During the summer, we got only around 2 million kyats per 100 baskets. Now it has doubled to 4 million. Prices need to stay at this level for us to survive next year.”
Compounding the crisis, heavy rains have triggered severe pest infestations—including onion thrips and rice bugs—alongside widespread rodent damage across Mon State’s paddy fields.
Meanwhile, market observers note that holding stock remains a gamble, as the new harvest is still several months away.
In August, the junta-controlled Myanmar Rice Federation issued a statement urging traders not to mark up stored stock and to sell rice at affordable rates to the public—an appeal that comes as tens of thousands of acres of farmland remain submerged by severe flooding.

title: Myanmar Junta Launches 1,000-Troop Offensive Along Sittwe-Ponnagyun Border
body:
The Myanmar military junta has launched a major offensive involving approximately 1,000 troops along the Sittwe-Ponnagyun border in western Myanmar's Rakhine State, triggering heavy clashes with the Arakan Army (AA), according to military sources.
Designated “Operation 4926,” the offensive began on Sept. 4 with five military columns—each comprising 170 to 200 soldiers—targeting key positions across Sittwe and Ponnagyun townships.
Military analysts say junta forces are attempting to cross the strategic Minchaung Bridge in Sittwe Township to establish a foothold in AA-controlled Ponnagyun and recapture lost territory.
However, after more than a week of intense fighting, several junta columns have suffered heavy casualties and been forced to retreat following AA counter-offensives.
Between Sept. 4 and Sept. 10, hundreds of junta soldiers, including column commanders, were reported killed or wounded.
“Both sides are exchanging heavy artillery and small arms fire. The military junta is also conducting airstrikes around active combat zones,” a military source said.
Junta forces have deployed extensive firepower, including heavy artillery, naval bombardment, combat drones, and airstrikes.
“The military junta is mounting large-scale offensives against territories controlled by the Arakan Army, but these operations are failing to achieve their objectives,” political analyst U Aung Marm Oo said. “Fighting is set to intensify further rather than diminish.”
The ongoing clashes come amid a broader push by the ethnic armed group to secure the region.
Arakan Army chief Maj. Gen. Twan Mrat Naing previously declared that revolutionary forces intend to liberate all remaining towns in Rakhine State before 2027.

title: Nearly 180,000 Displaced People in Myanmar’s Chin State Urgently Need Aid, Officials Say
body:
Nearly 180,000 people displaced by armed conflict in Myanmar’s western Chin State are in desperate need of food, medicine, and shelter, with the vast majority cut off from regular humanitarian assistance, according to local resistance officials.
The Chinland Council—the resistance-led governing authority in the region—reported that only about 40,000 displaced people currently have direct access to its aid operations, leaving more than 135,000 without consistent support.
“First and foremost, they need support for their livelihoods,” said Salai Za Thawng, Minister of Social Development for the Government of Chinland. “The second major need is tarpaulin sheets for shelter, alongside mosquito nets and medicine. We provide as much as we can, but it is still not enough.”
Fighting following the 2021 military coup has forced residents to flee into jungles, safer rural villages, neighboring Magway and Sagaing regions, and across the border into India's Mizoram State.
While many sheltering in India wish to return, ongoing military offensives, severe weather, and destroyed infrastructure make returning impossible.
Dr. Sharon Par, Minister of Health for the Chinland administration, noted that when factoring in those impacted by natural disasters alongside regime air raids and artillery strikes, the total number of refugees and internally displaced persons in Chin State approaches 200,000.
Chin resistance forces currently control much of the state, including key border towns and countryside, where they have established local healthcare, education, and administrative systems.
In response, the military regime has launched sustained ground offensives backed by heavy airstrikes and artillery barrages in an effort to retake lost territory.
